summary: A creeping herb from the parsley family, sold as “cica”. Its triterpenes (madecassoside, asiaticoside) are widely used in barrier and soothing products. The published human studies test multi-ingredient products or medical patients; none isolates Centella in everyday cosmetic use.

safetyNotes.note: Allergic contact dermatitis to Centella asiatica extract in cosmetics has been reported in case reports, including two recent patients from Turkey.

source.title: Allergic contact dermatitis from Centella asiatica extract and fragrance allergens: Report of two patients from Turkey (Contact Dermatitis 2024)

safetyNotes.note: In guinea pig testing, the raw extract and its triterpenes (asiaticoside, asiatic and madecassic acid) were very weak sensitisers, so sensitisation risk appears low.

source.title: Centella asiatica (Indian pennywort), an effective therapeutic but a weak sensitizer (Contact Dermatitis 1993)

summary: Finely milled whole oat (colloidal oatmeal) is a regulated skin protectant in the US and is labelled with its percentage. One vehicle-controlled trial supports it for dry skin; the other trials are in eczema or test whole products.

safetyNotes.note: Oat proteins in personal care products can cause immediate and delayed allergy, mostly reported in people with atopic dermatitis. Patch testing is suggested for atopic children.

source.title: Oat and wheat as contact allergens in personal care products (Dermatitis 2013)

safetyNotes.note: In a double-blind patch study of 65 young children, colloidal oat caused no allergic reactions. About 12% of atopic children had irritant reactions.

source.title: An evaluation of the allergic contact dermatitis potential of colloidal grain suspensions (Am J Contact Dermat 1997)

safetyNotes.note: Contact sensitisation from oat extracts in cosmetic creams has been reported in Belgium.

source.title: Sensitizing oat extracts in cosmetic creams: is there an alternative? (Contact Dermatitis 2010)

summary: Root extracts of two licorice species. Glycyrrhiza inflata supplies licochalcone A, studied for redness by its manufacturer; glabridin from G. glabra is studied for uneven tone. Most trials test multi-ingredient products.

safetyNotes.note: Allergic contact dermatitis to Glycyrrhiza inflata root extract has been reported, from an anti-acne cosmetic and from aftershave creams.

source.title: Allergic contact dermatitis to Glycyrrhiza inflata root extract in an anti-acne cosmetic product (Contact Dermatitis 2021)

safetyNotes.note: Allergic contact dermatitis to licorice root extract has also been reported in a US case report.

source.title: Allergic Contact Dermatitis to Licorice Root Extract (Dermatitis 2019)

safetyNotes.note: A case analysis identified licorice flavonoids as the contact allergens.

source.title: Contact allergy to liquorice flavonoids: analysis with liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (Contact Dermatitis 2016)

summary: Leaf extracts rich in catechins such as EGCG. A small meta-analysis supports topical extract for blemishes; other evidence is small, uncontrolled or combined with oral supplements.

safetyNotes.note: Immediate and delayed contact reactions to white and green tea blends have been reported.

source.title: Immediate and delayed contact reactions to white and green tea blends (Contact Dermatitis 2022)

safetyNotes.note: In a placebo-controlled photoaging trial, participants given green tea cream plus oral supplement reported more irritation than the placebo group.

source.title: Double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of green tea extracts in the clinical and histologic appearance of photoaging skin (Dermatol Surg 2005)

summary: A single molecule extracted from the seeds of Psoralea corylifolia, marketed as a gentler retinol alternative. One randomised trial compared it with retinol; a 2024 review rated the wider trial evidence at high risk of bias.

safetyNotes.note: Bakuchiol has been reported as a new cosmetic allergen causing allergic contact dermatitis.

source.title: Bakuchiol-A new allergen in cosmetics (Contact Dermatitis 2019)

safetyNotes.note: Further case reports describe contact dermatitis to bakuchiol in a cosmetic cream.

source.title: A new case of contact dermatitis to bakuchiol in a cosmetic cream (Contact Dermatitis 2020)

summary: Extracts of soybean seeds, including non-denatured soy with its protease inhibitors, studied for uneven tone and dullness. The main trial was vehicle-controlled but did not state randomisation.

safetyNotes.note: Protein contact dermatitis to soy has been reported to aggravate rosacea.

source.title: Aggravation of rosacea by protein contact dermatitis to soy (Contact Dermatitis 2005)

summary: A steam-distilled essential oil from the leaves of an Australian tree. Two randomised acne trials used a 5% gel; a 2023 systematic review judged the evidence modest. It is the essential oil most often reported to cause contact allergy.

safetyNotes.note: Among essential oils, tea tree oil has the most published allergic reactions. Oxidised (aged, air-exposed) oil is a stronger sensitiser than fresh oil.

source.title: Tea tree oil: contact allergy and chemical composition (Contact Dermatitis 2016)

safetyNotes.note: DermNet lists tea tree oil among essential oils that commonly cause allergic contact dermatitis, and advises patch testing with patients' own products.

source.title: Allergic contact dermatitis to essential oils (DermNet)

safetyNotes.note: A systematic review found mostly minor side effects, except with topical concentrations of 25% or more.

source.title: Efficacy and safety of Melaleuca alternifolia (tea tree) oil for human health-A systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Front Pharmacol 2023)

summary: The inner-leaf gel of Aloe barbadensis, mostly water and carbohydrates. Small studies support hydration and acute redness models; the acne trial was an add-on to a prescription retinoid.

safetyNotes.note: Patch testing of 702 consecutive patients with three aloe preparations produced no reactions. The inner-leaf gel is mostly carbohydrate and unlikely to sensitise.

source.title: Absence of contact sensitization to Aloe vera (L.) Burm. f. (Contact Dermatitis 2005)

safetyNotes.note: Allergic contact dermatitis has been reported with home-made whole-leaf aloe juice. Processed commercial gel usually excludes the irritant leaf-skin components.

source.title: Allergic contact dermatitis to Aloe vera (Contact Dermatitis 2007)

safetyNotes.note: A 2023 report examined contact allergens found in commercial aloe vera gels. Check the full ingredient list, not just the aloe.

source.title: Better Left Aloe? Contact Allergens in Aloe Vera Gels (Dermatitis 2023)

summary: Distillate and extracts of the North American shrub Hamamelis virginiana. Human evidence is limited to short UV-redness tests of the distillate; acne evidence is from cell culture only.

safetyNotes.note: Contact allergy to witch hazel has been reported, though published cases are few.

source.title: Contact allergy to witch hazel (Contact Dermatitis 1994)

summary: Pot marigold flowers, a member of the daisy family. A small irritation-model trial supports hydration; its best-known trials are in radiotherapy, where they disagree.

safetyNotes.note: Calendula is in the Compositae (Asteraceae) family. People with Compositae or sesquiterpene lactone allergy may react, and DermNet advises them to avoid Compositae-containing cosmetics.

source.title: Compositae allergy (DermNet)

safetyNotes.note: In 443 consecutive patch-tested patients, about 2% reacted to marigold. Standard Compositae or sesquiterpene mixes missed many of these sensitisations.

source.title: The seamy side of natural medicines: contact sensitization to arnica (Arnica montana L.) and marigold (Calendula officinalis L.) (Contact Dermatitis 2001)

safetyNotes.note: DermNet notes calendula sensitisation seems linked to medicinal use, and reports co-sensitisation to feverfew in a florist.

source.title: Marigold (DermNet)

summary: A daisy-family herb. Cosmetic use relies on extracts with parthenolide (a potent allergen) removed. Human data are short redness tests inside manufacturer laboratory papers.

safetyNotes.note: Parthenolide in feverfew is a potent contact allergen and a main cause of Compositae allergy. DermNet suggests products labelled purified or parthenolide-free.

source.title: Feverfew (DermNet)

safetyNotes.note: Four of seven feverfew-allergic patients reacted on patch testing to a cream with parthenolide-depleted extract. Depleted does not guarantee tolerance for allergic people.

source.title: Patch test reactivity to feverfew-containing creams in feverfew-allergic patients (Contact Dermatitis 2010)

safetyNotes.note: Feverfew is in the Compositae (Asteraceae) family. Cross-reactions with other Compositae plants such as chamomile and marigold are common.

source.title: Compositae allergy (DermNet)

summary: Oil pressed from the seeds of wild roses. The only topical trial found no effect, in a medical setting; benefits often quoted for skin ageing come from an oral supplement study, which says nothing about the oil on skin.

safetyNotes.note: Allergic contact dermatitis to rosa mosqueta (rosehip) oil has been reported.

source.title: Allergic contact dermatitis caused by "Rosa mosqueta" oil (Contact Dermatitis 2018)

summary: A pressed seed oil, rich in linoleic acid in many grades, used as an emollient. One small randomised forearm trial found it kept the skin barrier intact and improved hydration, while olive oil tested in the same study damaged it. That is the clearest reminder in this library that natural oils are not interchangeable. The oil comes from a daisy family plant, but refined seed oils carry little plant protein.

safetyNotes.note: In the same trial, olive oil applied twice daily for 4 to 5 weeks reduced stratum corneum integrity and caused mild redness in adults with and without a history of atopic dermatitis. Sunflower seed oil did not.

source.title: Effect of olive and sunflower seed oil on the adult skin barrier (Pediatr Dermatol 2013)

summary: A solid at room temperature seed oil used as a moisturiser. Two randomised trials compared virgin coconut oil with mineral oil: in mild to moderate dry skin the two performed comparably, and in children with atopic dermatitis coconut oil did better, but that is a medical setting. No trial tested it against no treatment on everyday healthy skin.

safetyNotes.note: Participants in the dry skin trial were patch tested first and only those with negative reactions took part. No adverse reactions were reported over 2 weeks. That says little about people who are prone to reacting.

source.title: Extra virgin coconut oil versus mineral oil as a moisturizer for xerosis (Dermatitis 2004)

summary: A kernel oil from Morocco used on skin and hair. One randomised trial in postmenopausal women found better skin elasticity measurements with daily argan oil, eaten and applied to the forearm, but the published abstract does not show that the topical part was compared with a control.

safetyNotes.note: A case report describes anaphylaxis after skin application of argan oil. This is rare, but it is a reason to patch test an oil you have not used before, especially if you have nut or seed allergies.

source.title: Anaphylaxis After Cutaneous Application of Argan Oil (J Investig Allergol Clin Immunol 2021)

summary: The seed of an annual herb used in Persian and Middle Eastern traditional medicine. A single randomised trial of a thymoquinone standardised hydrogel in people with acne found a large reduction in acne severity compared with a placebo gel. The effect is much larger than most acne trials show, so independent replication matters before relying on it.

safetyNotes.note: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis from a black cumin oil ointment, and severe contact dermatitis from Nigella sativa seed oil in beard cosmetics.

source.title: Allergic contact dermatitis from black cumin (Nigella sativa) oil-containing ointment (Contact Dermatitis 2002)

safetyNotes.note: A 2023 case report links severe allergic contact dermatitis to Nigella sativa seed oil in repeated contact with beard cosmetics.

source.title: Severe allergic contact connubial dermatitis to Nigella Sativa Seed Oil (Contact Dermatitis 2023)

summary: A shrub whose seed yields a liquid wax, used as a light oil. The only human study found here is an uncontrolled pilot of a clay and jojoba oil mask on acne prone skin, so the effect of jojoba itself cannot be separated from the clay.

scientificName: Source plant not stated in the trial (resveratrol occurs in grapes and Japanese knotweed)
summary: A single polyphenol found in grapes and some other plants, sold as an antioxidant. A recent randomised trial in women over 40 found fewer visible wrinkles only when resveratrol was both taken as a capsule and applied as a cream. The cream alone did not significantly change wrinkles, and it raised skin oil on the cheeks and jaw.

safetyNotes.note: In the 8 week trial, all products were safe with only minimal and mild adverse events in every group. The trial is short and in healthy women over 40.

source.title: Trans-resveratrol reduces visible signs of skin ageing in healthy adult females over 40 (Front Aging 2025)

commonName: Five leaf serratula (a plant source of arbutin)
summary: A daisy family plant whose leaves are a natural source of beta arbutin, a skin lightening compound. One randomised trial in women with melasma or sun spots found a cream with the leaf extract lightened and evened skin tone more than placebo. Arbutin on ingredient lists is more often made in a lab than taken from this plant, so this trial supports the extract, not every arbutin product.

safetyNotes.note: Serratula belongs to the daisy family (Asteraceae or Compositae). Contact allergy to Compositae plants is among the commonest plant allergies in Europe, with sesquiterpene lactones the main sensitisers. Whether this extract contains them is not stated in the trial abstract.

source.title: [Compositae dermatitis] (Med Pregl 2003)
